scenes.tts: What does a sensory nerve say about how hard you were touched? In 1926, Adrian and Zotterman recorded one stretch receptor in a frog muscle. They loaded the muscle with weights. The impulses never grew bigger. They only came more often.
scenes.visual: A weight chip grows from light to heavy beside a spike train; spikes keep one height but crowd closer together (in this sketch).
scenes.narration: What does a sensory nerve say about how hard you were touched? In 1926, Adrian and Zotterman recorded one stretch receptor in a frog muscle. They loaded the muscle with weights. The impulses never grew bigger. They only came more often.

scenes.tts: Every sense starts with transduction. It turns a stimulus into a receptor potential, a change in membrane voltage. The potential is graded: a stronger stimulus makes a larger one. Where the ending belongs to the afferent neuron, that voltage drives the spike initiating zone. The larger it is, the faster the neuron fires.
scenes.visual: Three stimulus strengths; the graded potential bar grows; the spike train beside each gets faster, spikes the same size.

scenes.tts: Endings also differ in time. A rapidly adapting ending fires at the start of a held stimulus, then falls quiet. Many fire again when it is removed. A slowly adapting ending keeps firing for as long as the stimulus lasts. So one reports change, and the other reports the stimulus itself.
scenes.visual: A held step stimulus above two spike trains: rapid ending fires at onset (and offset) only, slow ending fires throughout.
scenes.narration: Endings also differ in time. A rapidly adapting ending fires at the start of a held stimulus, then falls quiet. Many fire again when it is removed. scenes.tts: Plot firing against one stimulus, and you get a tuning curve. Here is a made-up neuron. It fires fifty spikes per second at zero degrees, and eight at forty five. You might expect it to be most useful at its peak. For telling nearby stimuli apart, it is often the reverse. The steepest part lies between fifteen and thirty degrees. With low, equal noise, a small change there moves the rate more. More noise can move the best place back toward the peak.

scenes.tts: Neighbours can also suppress a receptor. In the Limulus eye, lighting a unit's neighbours suppressed its steady discharge. Cutting the lateral connections abolished that inhibition. Now try a simple sketch. Each unit reports its own light minus point two times each neighbour's light. Ten, ten, ten, twenty, twenty, twenty becomes six, six, four, fourteen, twelve, twelve. The edge is exaggerated.

scenes.tts: Rate tells you how strong. Receptive fields tell you where. Quality is the harder question. In a labelled line, a fibre's activity means one thing, such as sweet. In a population code, quality is read from the pattern across many fibres. In smell, one odorant is recognized by several receptors, so it is coded by a combination. Taste researchers still argue between the two. Keep this: spikes look alike, so meaning lies in their rate, their source and their pattern.
scenes.visual: Labelled line (one fibre = sweet) beside a population pattern; odorant-receptor combination links; ends on the rule.
